catalog_quote: [p.35] Every word in Kuku Yalanji has primary stress on the first syllable, after which there is a distinct drop in pitch for disyllabic words and a more gradual drop for words of more than two syllables (see Hershberger & Pike 1970:791-792). Words with four or more syllables that are roots, reduplicated forms, or compounds, may have secondary stress on the third syllable, that is the first syllable of the second root in reduplicated forms of compounds. A reduplicated trisyllabic root may have secondary stress on the fourth syllable, again the first syllable of the second root. ... [p.36] But again, secondary stress is not obligatory and is in fact apparent only in slow and careful speech. In normal speech, even in long words of up to eight syllables, only the first syllable is stressed, with pitch subsiding over the following two or three syllables and remaining level over the rest. ... [p.6] Because of the attested close similarity between the dialects of Kuku Yalanji, the linguistic details described here may be taken to apply to the Kuku Yalanji language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word, with a pitch fall after it. Patz states this for Kuku Yalanji as a whole and explicitly lists Kuku Jangkun (Djangun) and Wakura among its dialects, so the rule applies to Djangun by her dialect claim, not from Djangun data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Optional, heard only in slow/careful citation forms: roots, reduplications and compounds of four or more syllables may take secondary stress on the third syllable (first syllable of the second root; fourth syllable for a reduplicated trisyllabic root); disyllabic suffixes take secondary stress on their first syllable; with monosyllabic suffixes/clitics a word of more than three syllables takes penultimate secondary stress unless that is the last root syllable. In normal speech only the first syllable is stressed even in words of up to eight syllables (pp.35-36).
new_statements.exceptions: None for primary stress. The adjective sequence -baja-ku 'very' is wholly unstressed (p.36). Clause stress also falls on the first syllable of a word (sec. 2.6.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('identifies a word as a unit'); compounds and reduplications are single phonological words with initial stress (p.22). Statement drawn from eastern Kuku Yalanji and Nyungkul speakers at Wujal Wujal (c.10 h texts + 19 h elicitation, 1979-81), not from Djangun speakers; Djangun itself is attested only in c.150 words (Dixon 1960s), the two Curr 1886 lists and Richards' 1926 Wakoora vocabulary.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog djan1238 Djangun = ISO djf = AUSTLANG Y109 Kuku Djangun/Djungan (Tindale 'Djankun', Dixon 'Dyangun (Dyangunbari)', Patz 'Kuku Jangkun'; Richards' 'Wakoora' = Patz's 'Wakura' dialect, 'almost identical' to Dyangun). Glottolog lists it as a separate Yalandyic language, but the only modern description, Patz 2002 (and AUSTLANG following Patz 1982), treats it as one of 13 dialects of Kuku Yalanji (kuku1273, AUSTLANG Y78); Dixon 1970:663 likewise says Wagaman-Dyangun-Muluridyi-Gugu-Yalandyi are 'probably all dialects of a single language'. The quoted stress statement is therefore a Kuku Yalanji statement (eastern Yalanji + Nyungkul data) applied to Djangun by the author's explicit dialect claim; a djan1238 catalog entry would inherit kuku1273's statement and the census merge bar should decide whether Djangun counts as a distinct language. No Djangun-specific phonology exists (AUSTLANG: grammar 0, text 0, word list <20 pp.).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word, with a pitch drop after it. Optional secondary stress, heard only in slow/careful citation speech: on the third syllable of roots, reduplications and compounds of four or more syllables (i.e. the first syllable of the second root; fourth syllable when a trisyllabic root is reduplicated); on the first syllable of disyllabic inflections/derivational suffixes; and, when monosyllabic suffixes or clitics make a word of more than three syllables, on the penultimate syllable unless that is the last root syllable. In normal speech only the first syllable is stressed, even in words of up to eight syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Optional and non-obligatory: 3rd syllable of 4+-syllable roots/reduplications/compounds (4th syllable of a reduplicated trisyllabic root); 1st syllable of disyllabic inflections or derivational suffixes; penultimate syllable of words of more than three syllables built with monosyllabic suffixes/clitics, unless the penult is the last root syllable (e.g. bama-ngka-ku, bulkiji-mun-bu-ku, yarraman-anda-ku-lu, p.63); 'usually omitted in other than careful citation forms' (p.62) and 'only apparent in very slow and careful speech' (p.63). Patz states her findings concur with Hershberger & Pike 1970 except where stated (p.61).
new_statements.exceptions: The suffix+clitic sequence -baja+ku 'very' on an adjective takes no stress at all (yalbay-baja-ku, p.63; Patz rejects Hershberger/Pike's treatment of bajaku as a separate word because of this consistent absence of stress). Monosyllabic inflections, derivational suffixes and clitics are unstressed. Later in the grammar (sec. 3.2.3, ca. p.109 of the layout text) reduplicated stems like mala-minya are said to vary: sometimes the first stem syllable is stressed, more often only the first root syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Patz 1982 describes eastern Kuku Yalanji and Kuku Nyungkul (Bloomfield River / Wujal Wujal); Kuku Jangkun (= Dixon's Dyangun/Dyangunbari, Tindale's Djankun) is one of the 13 dialects in her Table 1.1 (p.6) and Map 2, and the stress statement reaches it only through her p.8 claim that the description applies to the whole Kuku Yalanji language. No Djangun-speaker data appears in the thesis. Glottolog treats Djangun as a separate language (djan1238); AUSTLANG Y109 and Patz treat it as a Kuku Yalanji dialect. Dixon 1966 and 1991 are about Mbabaram (mbab1239); Dixon's 1966 footnotes mention a single Dyangun informant, Willie Richards.

sources.citation: Richards, Francis. 1926. Customs and language of the Western Hodgkinson Aboriginals. Memoirs of the Queensland Museum 8(3): 249-265.
sources.note: 'Wakoora' tribe of Mt Mulligan; 'Language' section pp.258-259 gives four sentences of grammar and a c.800-word vocabulary 'written as pronounced'. Entries carry acute accents, mostly on the first syllable (Kúrrngun, Chóoma, Bútta, Múmmarra, Kóorchoo, Yálla..), a few later (Marróon, Wanchámba, nookárnga, Nagóoroo, Yukkóoey), but the paper never states what the accents mark; no sentence on accent or stress anywhere (pp.249-265 checked).

Classification Pama-Nyungan > Yimidhirr-Yalanji-Yidinic > Yalandyic; subclassification comment cites Patz 2002; no grammar/sketch/phonology references (the number of descriptive works Glottolog lists 0).
